newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian PM says sorry for "stolen" Aborigines.
newsitem.headline: Australian PM says sorry for "stolen" Aborigines.

text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard made an unexpected personal apology on Monday to tens of thousands of Aborigines forcibly taken from their parents under a past government policy of assimilation.

Australia's Human Rights Commission has called the assimilation policy that existed from the 1880s to the 1960s attempted genocide and has called for a formal government apology and compensation to the "Stolen Generation" Aborigines.

"Personally, I feel deep sorrow for those of my fellow Australians who suffered injustices under the practices of past generations towards indigenous people," Howard said in opening the Aboriginal Reconciliation Convention in Melbourne.

"I am sorry for the hurt, the trauma, many here today may continue to feel as a consequence of those practices," Howard told a mainly hostile Aboriginal audience of around 1,500 delegates gathered to discuss strained black-white relations.
Howard won loud applause for his apology, but drew jeers when he said Australian history since white settlement in 1788 was not a history of "imperialism and exploitation and racism".
Hundreds of delegates stood and turned their back on Howard as he continued his speech, which stressed better Aboriginal living standards, not "gestures", was the key to reconcilation.
Howard implied race row politician Pauline Hanson and her right-wing One Nation party had hindered better Aboriginal relations, but said reconciliation should not be based on guilt.
"Australians of this generation should not be required to accept guilt and shame for past practices over which they had no control," Howard said, provoking cries of protest.
Council for Aboriginal Reconciliation chairman Pat Dodson welcomed Howard's apology but said the nation's parliament must follow suit. "It's a good start," Dodson told reporters.
Parliamentarians in Canberra, including Hanson, stood for a minute's silence on Monday out of respect for the Aborigines taken from parents as children between the 1880s and 1960s.
Only one government legislator refused to stand.
Aborigines taken from their parents are demanding a formal apology and compensation, but the government has so far shied away from the question of compensation.
The government plans to release a human rights report on the "Stolen Generation" on Wednesday.
Dodson told the conference the outcome of the "Stolen Generation" issue and the government's stance on indigenous title to land were crucial to reconciliation with Aborigines.

"We can compensate for forcing people to hand in their guns and we now have to find a way to compensate those who were taken away (from parents)," said Dodson, referring to gun laws introduced after last year's mass killings in Tasmania state.
Dodson rejected Howard's compromise plan on indigenous title to pastoral land. The plan seeks to limit a recent High Court decision giving Aborigines the right to share land with farmers.
"If we cannot achieve co-existence, then we cannot achieve reconciliation," Dodson told the conference.

Earlier, in a traditional ceremony which set the tone for the conference, Howard presented a smouldering heap of leaves to an Aboriginal elder to signify he was a guest on her land. An Aboriginal woman then jumped on the stage and harangued him.

The Council for Aboriginal Reconciliation convened the conference to help it fulfill its duty to produce a "national agreement of reconciliation" by the year 2000. Such an agreement could be written into the constitution, under one proposal.

About 1,800 Aboriginal, political, business and community delegates will try over the next three days to reach a common view on issues that have plagued relations for up to 200 years. These views would then form the basis of a future agreement.
